title: Buy the Competitor to Buy Yourself Time
documentTitle: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech) — PTX0058: Email from Neal Mohan to Jason Harinstein (October 11, 2010)
excerptForBlog:
3) What do you guys think about acquiring one of them? Is that like giving up before trying? I am concerned that it will take a long time to sort out the org stuff internally. One way to make sure we dont get further behind in the market is picking up the one with the most traction and parking it somewhere.

Scott and I have not talked much about this yet. I have come around to believing we should go into due diligence and probably make a buy. It does not solve a ton of problems by itself, but as you say if we bought one and parked it, it would let us solve the problems from a position of strength (market share, knowledgeable team members). Kind of like how we had time to build XFP because DFP was doing so well. The biggest problem is having two inventory pools (AdX and YM-RTB system) which if we leave it up could be confusing to buyers and to publishers deciding which to use; or if we tried to combine them fast could yield a Falk-like situation (a mix of advantages and feature gaps, and some pubs upset about what they lose).

looks like there is going to be interest in YM. if we go down that path it will become my top priority like invite was. maybe the first thing we should do is have a prelim meeting (you and i probably) with their CEO.

lessonTitle: Buy the Competitor to Buy Yourself Time
pullQuote: Sometimes you acquire a rival not to use what they built, but to stop the clock while you fix what you have.
situation: In October 2010, Google executive Neal Mohan emailed a colleague about whether Google should acquire one of its competitors in the ad exchange space. The internal debate: was buying someone an admission of failure, or a smart way to stay competitive while Google sorted out messy organizational problems?
insight: Mohan's key move is separating two things people usually confuse: solving the problem vs. buying time to solve it from a better position. He writes that an acquisition 'does not solve a ton of problems by itself' — but it would let Google 'solve the problems from a position of strength (market share, knowledgeable team members).' That's a precise strategic distinction. He's not buying a solution; he's buying a stable foundation. He even draws a direct parallel: Google 'had time to build XFP because DFP was doing so well.' One strong asset funded the runway to build the next one. He also flags the real risk clearly — two competing inventory pools (AdX and the target's system) could confuse buyers and publishers, or a rushed integration could create a 'Falk-like situation' with feature gaps and unhappy customers. He names the downside before he commits. That's disciplined thinking, not wishful deal-making. The underlying framework here is **competitive moats**: you acquire to protect existing position, not just to add revenue.
application: Before your next acquisition or partnership conversation, write one sentence answering this: 'What specific position does this buy us time to defend or build?' If you can't write that sentence, the deal is probably solving the wrong problem. If you can, make sure you also name the integration risk — Mohan's 'Falk-like situation' warning — before you walk into the first meeting.
